title: Cynthia & Kelly:
length: about 90 s (about 75 s without the two optional rows)
headline: When someone walks out of prison and through their door, two peers who run the Omaha house say: “Welcome home.”
story: Cynthia runs MHA's Omaha house. Kelly is a peer support specialist there. Their favorite moment is when somebody gets out of prison and walks through the door. Some cry. Some feel they do not deserve the space. “And we're just like, welcome home.”

They know it from the inside: labels, small steps, and a job that is “for the people”. It must feel warm, close and hopeful. The two of them together is the point, so it starts and ends on both of them.
do: Open on frame 1 with both women on the couch, already talking.
Keep both in frame for the hook and the last lines.
Match every line to the right woman by voice before you caption it.
Two name supers, each on her own intro line.
Cut clean around every laugh and every tear.
dont: Never use crying, laughing or “cut that out” moments as a beat.
No “criminal charges” in any headline or hook text.
No WRAP answers (08:30–12:27). They belong to the WRAP video.
No prison footage and no stock images of a prison.

voice.quote: For me, recovery has to happen in like really small steps. … My recovery started with, today I'm going to get out of bed and go brush my teeth. … I think that recovery looks different for everybody.

voice.quote: This job is not for the money. This job is for the people. This job is about walking with people through the hardest steps of their life, quite possibly.

rows.visual: Back to the 2-shot. Both of them together is the point. Hold on the 2-shot to the end. Cut every laugh and every “cut that out” around these lines.
rows.motion: Captions only. Each short line gets its own caption.

voice.quote: Hope looks like freedom. … hope looks like recovery. … Peer support is powerful because I can be my authentic self. … I love MHA. … It changed my life.

rows.music: Gentle peak. Resolve on “It changed my life.”

transcript:
Auto-transcript of 20260910_C4825.MP4 (Cynthia and Kelly, Terrapin Station, Omaha, 10 Sep 2026). Times are mm:ss in the source file. The transcript has no speaker names. Match each line to Cynthia or Kelly by voice: Cynthia introduces herself at 00:23 and 12:48, Kelly at 00:31 and 12:52. Laughing, crying and "cut that out" chatter is marked and must never be used.
[00:05] (Before the interview, 00:05–00:18.)
[00:23] Oh, we both I'm Cynthia, I'm the coordinator for Omaha.
[00:31] I'm Kelly, I'm a peer support specialist for Omaha.
[00:36] (Interviewer) How did you first come across MHA?
[00:40] So I was working at a different transitional living facility. And my co worker had gone to the VLS quarterly meeting and met Tessa and MHA was there presenting their expansion to Omaha. And she encouraged me to leave the job I was at and call Tessa immediately. And so that's what I did.
[01:06] I heard about this through my friend Kristen. And I thought it was amazing. And it ended up being a perfect fit for me.
[01:17] (Interviewer) What makes peer support different from traditional support?
[01:26] (Pause and chatter, 01:26–01:30.)
[01:31] To me, intentional peer support is really like, to me, it's all about the whole person.
[01:42] For me, I was always labeled with a diagnosis or identified by my criminal charges or what the courts thought of me.
[01:51] And when I took intentional peer support, I was like, wow, that's not who I am.
[01:56] It's all about the things that have happened to me.
[02:00] And to me, a lot of people help and they don't support.
[02:04] And there's a big difference to me in that supporting, we're able to do things together and to work through things together versus me kind of being this expert in whatever they need help in and me giving them the answers.
[02:17] Now I can just walk alongside people and I really enjoy that.
[02:21] (Chatter and tears, 02:21–02:36.)
[02:37] (Interviewer) Tell me a moment that you still think about whether it's with coworkers or participants.
[02:47] (02:47–03:09: "My boss right here", tears, "cut all that out". Never use.)
[03:11] I think for me, just seeing people step up and be in our community and be really involved and care about the space that we're in.
[03:20] But my favorite moment is just when somebody gets out of prison and comes through that door and the look on their face, some of them cry. Some of them feel like they're not deserving to be in this space. And we're just like, welcome home.
[03:34] (Chatter and tears, 03:34–03:52.)
[03:55] (Interviewer) What would you say to someone who doesn't believe they can recover?
[04:01] Yes, you can recover. You can. I did it. I know many people that have done it. A lot of my friends are going through it right now. Recovery is possible.
[04:19] For me, recovery has to happen in like really small steps.
[04:24] The very first time I tried to get clean, I had so much guilt and shame that I couldn't even get out of bed.
[04:32] My recovery started with, today I'm going to get out of bed and go brush my teeth.
[04:38] I created that small habit for a week. The next week it was, I'm going to get out of bed, I'm going to brush my teeth, and I'm going to take a shower. That was what my recovery looked like.
[04:51] My brain just couldn't wrap its mind around staying clean for more than 30 seconds.
[04:57] I had to take my recovery into really small steps.
[05:00] I think that recovery looks different for everybody.
[05:04] (Interviewer) What do people get wrong about this job?
[05:25] This job is not for the money. This job is for the people. This job is about walking with people through the hardest steps of their life, quite possibly.
[05:45] That's what it's all about, to me.
[05:50] I think for me, what people get wrong or maybe what the hardest part is, is when you see somebody's what you believe is their potential and they're totally on a different path. You want to be like, stop, don't go that way. That's wrong because you can't learn a lesson or learn anything in life if you're not allowed to make choices.
[06:16] When people talk about transitional living or reentry, they think that we're setting goals and doing things for people. That's not what we're doing.
[06:24] We're creating informed choices for people and allowing them to take the wheel on their life, which they've never been allowed to do.
[06:31] People have made decisions for them in rooms that they were never allowed to be in.
[06:37] We don't do that here.
[06:39] (Chatter, 06:39–06:42.)
[06:43] (Interviewer) If someone watching has never heard of MHA, what should they know?
[06:53] We're amazing. I said this at my very first All Staff, and two years later, it is still true that I 100% believe that everybody I work with is the same person when they clock in as when they clock out. I don't question anybody's integrity here. I believe that our mission lives in people's hearts when they go home.
[07:16] (Chatter, 07:16–07:29.)
[07:30] (Interviewer) Someone watching has never heard of MHA ... What's one thing you would tell them, or what should they know about MHA?
[07:47] I help people during the toughest times of their lives.
[07:51] I get to sit down with them and hear what's going on with them and how they're doing and the stories of their lives, and there's nothing more.
[08:03] I go home, and I'm still thinking about it, and I'm laying in bed, and I'm like, how are they doing? When they leave here, I'm still wondering, how are you doing?
[08:13] There's no other job that I have ever had that you can really know people, get to know people. That's what MHA is to me.
[08:30] (Interviewer) How has RAP impacted your life? (Chatter and tears, 08:36–08:44.)
[08:44] So RAP, I had never, I had heard of it, but I didn't really know what it was, and when they said that it was a plan created by me for me, I still didn't really understand what it meant, because I've been in spaces where people created safety plans for me to prevent me from using or making poor decisions in their mind or going to a hospital, and so there was always a safety plan in place, but it was, call the doctor, call the ambulance, call the meds, call, you know, all these things, lock her up, and I, RAP opened my mind that I have control over decisions that are being made for me. Like, I have a voice in that, and there were some things that, like, I love that we took it together, and I got to take it with all my coworkers, because I learned different ways that people experience wellness and different ways that they experience when they're not okay, and I think that it brought us closer together, because now, like, now I know some of the things that Kelly has said, that when I'm not okay, this is what happens, and we can have a conversation about that, and to really just be in tune with yourself and with other people is, it's great.
[10:02] (Chatter, 10:02–10:22. Never use.)
[10:24] When I first did RAP, I was in rehab, and it was actually traumatic for me. I was handed this thick packet, and it had all these really in-depth, serious questions for me, and I was scared of it, and they sent me to sit down, and when I did RAP at MHA, I, like Cynthia said, I sat down in a group with awesome people, my coworkers and my friends, and I found out what it really was.
[11:00] (Tears and chatter, 11:00–11:46. Never use.)
[11:47] I think it has impacted the culture, because MHA is all about informed choice and allowing people to take their own power back and to be able to make choices for themselves. We are surrounded by people who have been told what to do for a very long time, and RAP gives them that power back that, like, I trust you to make your own decisions, even if I don't agree with it, and it might not be the decision that I would make, I trust that you know what's best for you.
[12:22] (Chatter, 12:22–12:47.)
[12:48] My name is Cynthia, and I am a coordinator at MHA.
[12:52] My name is Kelly, and I'm a peer support specialist at MHA.
[13:00] (Interviewer) The next sentence is, hope looks like, take it away.
[13:06] Hope looks like freedom.
[13:13] They're all important, but hope looks like recovery.
[13:27] Peer support is powerful because everybody needs somebody.
[13:37] (Restarts and laughing, 13:37–13:56. Never use.)
[13:57] Peer support is powerful because I get to be who I am authentically.
[14:05] (Chatter, 14:05–14:23.)
[14:24] Peer support is powerful because I can be my authentic self.
[14:33] (Interviewer) Anything else you guys want to add or share?
[14:37] I love MHA.
[14:39] I do too.
[14:40] It changed my life.
[14:42] Same.
[14:44] (After the interview, 14:44–15:28. Never use.)
